props.title: Duplicity

sections.content: Duplicity brilliantly revives sophisticated corporate espionage thrillers with crackling chemistry between Julia Roberts and Clive Owen. Director Tony Gilroy, fresh off Michael Clayton (2007), crafts an intricate puzzle box of double-crosses and time jumps that recalls classic con films like The Thomas Crown Affair (1968). The film's opening sequence - a slow-motion face-off between rival CEOs in the rain - immediately establishes its playful tone while nodding to the glamorous spy capers of the 1960s like Charade (1963).

sections.content: Gilroy's screenplay masterfully weaves corporate intrigue with romantic comedy, following the pattern established by classic films like To Catch a Thief (1955). The constant question of trust between Roberts' and Owen's characters creates delicious tension, while the corporate warfare backdrop provides a modern twist on traditional spy narratives. The film's structure, with its complex flashbacks, draws from noir traditions seen in Out of Sight (1998) and The Usual Suspects (1995).

The film's visual style deserves special attention, with cinematographer Robert Elswit creating a glossy, high-stakes world reminiscent of Catch Me If You Can (2002). The corporate settings become architectural playgrounds for deception, while the intimate scenes between the leads echo the sophisticated romantic thrillers of the 1960s like North by Northwest (1959). sections.content: Duplicity represents a key evolution in corporate thrillers, building on foundations laid by films like Wall Street (1987) and The Firm (1993). Its approach to industrial espionage feels particularly prescient now, predating real-world corporate security concerns that would emerge in films like Blackhat (2015) and Zero Days (2016).
